articles.title: El Paso investigators detail 9 years of alleged restroom spying by 'peeping tom'
articles.description: El Paso deputies arrest alleged 'peeping tom' after gas station restroom incident EL PASO, Texas (KFOX14/CBS4) -- Police documents show more "peeping tom" allegations against the 36-year-old man who was arrested on July 2 for allegedly spying on a woman in a gas station restroom. The complaint affidavit for Ivan Abraham Ponce lists and describes in detail several instances in the past nine years where he allegedly either spied on or recorded women in public restrooms. The most recent one (and the one previously reported) happened on June 29, at around 9:36 a.m., at a Circle K gas station on 12281 Eastlake Blvd. in the Lower Valley. According to the affidavit, deputies with the El Paso County Sheriff's Office answered the call and spoke with the victim, who said she was in a stall when she heard footsteps, "a slapping noise," and heavy breathing. The victim said she got scared, feeling like someone was spying on her, and so she pulled her garments up and waited in the stall until she heard footsteps leaving the restroom. In the affidavit, deputies describe watching surveillance video from the gas station, which appears to show Ponce hanging out outside the restrooms before following a woman inside. Snippets from the surveillance video were then shared on the popular social media account @therealfitfamelpaso. WATCH: Deputies stated that they recognized Ponce, noting that he worked at the El Cometa on 9529 Viscount Blvd. in East El Paso. With the suspect identified, deputies said they ran a history check on Ponce, learning about four more incidents allegedly involving Ponce doing the same thing in other public restrooms, twice in the same restaurant. Previous incidents The affidavit alleges that on Dec. 10, 2025, and March 30, 2025, two incidents were reported at the restaurant Rudy's located at 7970 Gateway East Blvd. in the Lower Valley. Following the most recent incident at the Circle K, investigators met with some of the victims. In the affidavit, investigators describe their conversation with the manager of Rudy's. She alleges that she was inside a stall in the restroom when she spotted Ponce looking at her through the crack by the wall. "Hey, somebody is in here," the victim recalls saying before chasing after him; however, she said that by the time she stepped out, Ponce had left the restaurant. The manager also told investigators that she saved the surveillance video from that day in case Ponce ever came back, and she alleges that he did some months later and did the same thing to another woman. This time, the victim, who was 18 years old, was reportedly in the restroom recording a "TikTok" video when she saw a cellphone flash as if someone was taking photo or video of her. On Dec. 8, 2019, the affidavit alleges that Ponce went into the women's restroom at the Starr Western Wear store located at 750 Sunland Park Dr. and recorded a woman. On August 4, 2017, the affidavit alleges Ponce was cited for going into the women's restroom at 4849 N. Mesa St. and peeping into a stall. Questions It is unclear what happened in the investigations surrounding those previous incidents at Rudy's. The cases were opened by the El Paso Police Department, but according to the affidavit, investigators found that they were inactive. According to the affidavit, the investigator reached out to EPPD to adopt the case where Ponce allegedly recorded the woman inside the Rudy's restaurant. KFOX14/CBS4 reached out to EPPD to learn why the cases were inactive. And while police couldn't comment on the cases, an EPPD spokesperson told us that when a case is "inactive," it doesn't mean it's closed, but just that, for various reasons, like lack of information, the investigation has been paused. Below is EPPD's full statement: An inactive case is not a closed case, and there can be many reasons why a case is inactive. I can't tell you the exact reason for the cases you are inquiring about, however some reasons could be that the investigator has paused the investigation pending more leads, there may not be enough workable information to make an arrest, all potential investigative steps have already been explored and sometimes there is limited cooperation from complainants or witnesses. Again, this is just in general and not specifically to the cases you are inquiring about. What's next? Jail records show Ponce was booked into the El Paso County Downtown Jail on Tuesday, where he was charged with two counts of voyeurism and one count of invasive visual recording. According to jail records, Ponce remains in jail under a combined bond of $320,000. Court records show a bond hearing is scheduled for Ponce for Thursday morning. pendingReview.title: Police Used Flock's License Plate Network to Stalk Women in at Least 50 Cases
pendingReview.description: Officers need no warrant and no case number to search a woman's movements across 120,000 cameras Marci Bakely, a 50-year-old single mother in Jefferson, Georgia, typed her license plate number into a website called Have I Been Flocked and learned what she had already suspected: her ex-boyfriend, Michael Steffman, the police chief of nearby Braselton, had queried her vehicle and her teenage daughter's vehicle through Flock Safety's AI-powered license plate reader network roughly 600 times over the course of a year, according to the IJ tracker. No warrant had been required. No case number. No active investigation. The system allowed it because Steffman, like every officer at a Flock-contracted department, could enter a vehicle into a search field, type the word "investigation" as his reason, and be done. What distinguished his 600 queries from a legitimate criminal inquiry was nothing the database could see. Bakely's case is not an anomaly. It is, according to a Washington Post investigation published August 3, one of at least 50 documented cases across the United States in which law enforcement officers have been charged with or accused of misusing AI-powered automated license plate reader systems to conduct unauthorized surveillance of intimate partners, ex-partners, or women they wanted to meet. In 26 of those cases, prosecutors and investigators concluded that officers used the technology specifically to spy on wives, girlfriends, former partners, their exes' new partners, or women they sought to approach. The Washington Post based its findings on an analysis of police and court records nationwide, reported by Drew Harwell, Douglas MacMillan, and Aaron Schaffer. What makes police-enabled surveillance through Flock structurally different from the GPS trackers, AirTags, and stalkerware apps more commonly associated with domestic abuse is this: the officer does not need to install anything, access any device, or touch the victim at all. Flock's network of more than 120,000 roadside cameras records every vehicle that passes -- 20 billion plate scans per month -- in a searchable, time-stamped database accessible to law enforcement users without judicial authorization. A single search query recruits that entire network as a passive tracking apparatus. An officer who sets a specific plate on a "hot list" receives an automatic alert whenever that vehicle appears anywhere in the system -- across city limits, across state lines, across jurisdictions the officer has no authority in. The abuser does not need to be present. The cameras do the watching for him. How Officers Transformed a Crime-Fighting Tool Into a Surveillance Weapon Flock Safety's cameras were built for a narrower purpose: helping police recover stolen vehicles and investigate crimes. Each shoebox-size unit runs Android, connects to Flock's servers via LTE, and uses computer vision to extract not just a license plate number but a full "vehicle fingerprint" -- make, model, color, body style, bumper stickers, roof racks, and visible damage -- at vehicle speeds up to 100 mph (161 km/h), in low light, and in rain. Officers search the resulting database in natural language through Flock's FreeForm system, typing descriptions like "blue pickup truck with a kayak in the bed." The architecture that enables stalking is not a flaw in that system. It is the system. Officers with authorized access log in with personal credentials, enter any plate number, type a reason for the search, and receive a location history. The reason field accepts anything, including a single word. In the Milwaukee case that first drew national attention, Officer Josue Ayala -- an eight-year Milwaukee Police Department veteran -- ran 179 unauthorized searches over a two-month span in 2025: 55 queries for the plate of a woman he was dating and 124 for the plate of her ex-partner. Every one of those 179 searches was logged under the reason code "investigation." The Wisconsin Examiner found that "investigation" was the most common justification Wisconsin agencies used to access Flock data across the first five months of 2025. When one of Ayala's victims looked up her plate on HaveIBeenFlocked.com and saw the query history, the investigation began. The Flock database that Ayala accessed is the same one available to some 140,000 active users across more than 6,000 communities in the United States. Officers operate at every rank, in every type of agency, across departments with wildly varying policies on how Flock searches must be documented and what ratio of queries are audited. In many jurisdictions, there is no requirement that a search be tied to a case number, no automatic flag when the same plate is queried repeatedly by the same officer, and no notification sent to the vehicle's owner. Why This Is Structurally Different From Stalkerware Domestic abuse advocates have documented for years how commercially available surveillance tools -- GPS trackers, AirTags, spyware -- are used by abusers to track partners. Flock creates a different problem. Sociologist Evan Stark, whose landmark book on coercive control defined the modern understanding of domestic abuse as a pattern of domination rather than isolated incidents of violence, identified surveillance as a central mechanism through which abusers maintain control long after a relationship has ended -- including, specifically, covert location monitoring. What Flock enables is technology-facilitated coercive control using state infrastructure, with three asymmetries that no consumer product can replicate. First, scale: a stalker with an AirTag can track one vehicle. A Flock-authorized officer can set a hot-list alert on a vehicle and have 120,000 cameras across the country reporting its location automatically. Second, legitimacy: consumer stalkerware, if discovered, is evidence of criminal stalking. A Flock search logged as "investigation" looks, in the audit log, like law enforcement work -- at least until someone pulls the full query history and notices a pattern. Third, reporting: a civilian victim of stalkerware can report the conduct to police. A victim of officer-facilitated Flock surveillance faces the question Bakely asked aloud: "Who do you turn the police chief in to?" The Institute for Justice, which tracks documented ALPR stalking cases and is representing plaintiffs challenging ALPR networks in San Jose and Norfolk, has identified dozens of named cases nationwide as of August 3, 2026, and describes its tracker as "almost certainly an undercount." Attorney Michael Soyfer put the structural cause plainly: "The fundamental problem with these systems is that they place private information about people's movements over time in the hands of every officer. Without the constitutional safeguard of a warrant requirement, that predictably allows officers to abuse their access to these systems for things like stalking romantic partners." Case by Case: What the Pattern Looks Like Across States The 50 cases documented in the Washington Post investigation follow a recognizable pattern regardless of state or rank: an officer with authorized access, a personal motivation, and no friction between intent and surveillance. But the details reveal the range of harm the system enables. In Wisconsin, a Menasha police officer named Cristian Morales used Flock to check whether his then-girlfriend had visited a clinic to "seek a potential termination of said pregnancy," according to an affidavit from an investigating officer seeking to subpoena Flock's search records. Morales texted the woman to say he had confirmed she had not gone to the clinic and told her, "You continue to lie." He then contacted the clinic attempting to obtain her medical records, confronted her at her home, and began calling her as many as 19 times a day. His case is scheduled for trial this month. In Kansas, a police chief tracked his estranged wife's vehicle through Flock and used the resulting location data to appear at her location while she was intimate with another man -- conduct that a state police certification body concluded contributed to his firing. In Florida, a Monroe County sheriff's deputy allegedly added a young actress he had met while working security on a television production to a Flock hot list and received an automatic alert when her vehicle appeared in the network. He sped to intercept her -- a sequence captured on his dashboard camera -- and nearly caused a head-on collision. He was arrested in March 2026. A Guardian alert -- a competing ALPR product from a different vendor -- was the specific tool used in that case. In California, former Riverside County Sheriff's Deputy Alexander Vanny used Flock as part of a months-long campaign of stalking and harassment against his former fiancée -- a campaign that also involved installing a hidden camera in her roommate's bathroom. Vanny was convicted on 10 charges, including stalking and unauthorized access to electronic data, and was sentenced in February 2026 to six years in prison. In Georgia -- where the Institute for Justice and Reason.com have documented 18 officer arrests across multiple counties for Flock database misuse -- the scale of the problem forced a statewide reckoning. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation arrested five former Albany Police Department officers on July 6, 2026, on charges of Misuse of License Plate Data and Violation of Oath of Office after an internal audit found repeated non-law-enforcement searches. The wave of arrests included officers in Albany, Cherokee County, Fayetteville, Richmond County, Greene County, and Conyers. In Milwaukee, weeks after Ayala's case became public, one of the internal affairs detectives assigned to investigate him was himself charged with misusing Flock to track two people -- and with separately placing a GPS device on one victim's vehicle. Can Victims Discover If They Have Been Tracked? In most cases documented in the Washington Post investigation, victims discovered the surveillance only after they felt something was wrong -- and took action themselves. The primary discovery tool is the Have I Been Flocked site, maintained by civil liberties advocates that aggregates publicly available Flock audit logs from police departments that release them through public records requests. Bakely used it. One of Ayala's victims used it. What the website's existence reveals is how narrow the transparency window actually is. Not all departments make Flock audit logs publicly available. Some release them only in response to formal public records requests, which require knowing the relevant jurisdiction and filing correctly. The logs, when obtained, show search queries -- but they show only what officers recorded as their reason, which is self-reported and unvalidated. A search logged as "investigation" is indistinguishable in the audit log from an actual investigation unless someone pulls the full query history, compares the volume of searches to any known case, and notices the pattern. The Milwaukee Police Department, responding to the Ayala case, revoked most officers' access and instituted more detailed audit requirements. That response was not Flock-initiated. It was departmental, reactive, and limited to one city. Flock Safety itself introduced a voluntary audit assistance tool in April 2026 -- a feature that scans for suspicious search patterns, such as repeated queries for a single vehicle or queries made outside an officer's working hours. But the feature is optional. Individual departments decide whether to adopt it. Flock CEO Garrett Langley acknowledged the limits of what the company can prevent: "We're not going to change humans, and humans make bad decisions. What we can do is make sure that they know if you use this tool, you will be held accountable." Eva Galperin of the Electronic Frontier Foundation pushed back on that framing: "Flock has already claimed that they have oversight, that they have guardrails, and we still see these kinds of abuses." What the Law Does and Does Not Require The fundamental governance gap that makes officer-enabled Flock stalking possible is not a bug in the system's design. It is an absence in the legal framework governing the system's use. No federal statute requires law enforcement officers to obtain a warrant before querying an ALPR database. No federal law mandates that ALPR searches be tied to active investigations. No federal rule limits how many times a single officer can search the same plate, or requires notification of the vehicle owner when a search occurs. In the absence of federal law, states have moved unevenly. Six states -- California, Colorado, Washington, Utah, Kentucky, and Maine -- have enacted ALPR-specific legislation imposing various combinations of data retention limits, warrant requirements for certain uses, and prohibitions on sharing data with federal agencies. About 35 states have enacted no comprehensive ALPR-specific law. Florida, which has more than 100 law enforcement agencies holding Flock contracts and an estimated 7,500 cameras statewide, has no state law restricting how officers may use ALPR data. At the federal level, Republican Texas Representative Keith Self introduced the Protecting Rights in Video and Equipment Acquired Discovery (PRIVACY) Act on July 15, 2026 -- legislation that would require federal law enforcement agencies to obtain a warrant before querying surveillance data collected by state and local systems, including ALPR networks. The bill is cosponsored by Representatives Eli Crane of Arizona and Andrew Clyde of Georgia. It addresses only federal agency access to local data -- it would not, as written, impose a warrant requirement on the kind of individual officer searches documented in the Washington Post investigation. The constitutional question at the core of these cases is currently before the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals in Schmidt v. City of Norfolk, with the ACLU and EFF having filed a joint amicus brief in April 2026. Their argument draws on the Supreme Court's 2018 ruling in Carpenter v. United States -- which held that acquiring seven or more days of historical cell-site location information is a Fourth Amendment search requiring a warrant, because the data is "detailed, encyclopedic, and effortlessly compiled." The ACLU and EFF argue that a network logging every vehicle's movements across 120,000 cameras generates exactly the kind of comprehensive location record Carpenter was designed to protect. Two January 2026 lower-court rulings -- Schmidt v. City of Norfolk in federal district court and State v. Simonson in Washington State's Court of Appeals -- upheld limited ALPR deployments without a warrant, but both courts noted that the constitutional calculus could shift as camera density increases. The Supreme Court has not ruled on an ALPR case. Steffman and the Limits of Accountability Marci Bakely sought a restraining order after confronting Steffman with the audit logs. A judge denied it, finding insufficient evidence of ongoing abuse. Steffman was eventually arrested on stalking, harassment, and ALPR misuse charges. Before his case reached trial, he was found dead at his home in April 2026 in what officials described as a suicide. Bakely's experience illustrates a compound failure that appears throughout the documented cases. The victim cannot see the surveillance in real time -- only retrospectively, through a public records tool that aggregates logs some agencies release and others do not. The reporting mechanism requires the victim to approach an institution that may be the same institution employing her abuser. The evidentiary standard for a civil protective order may not account for a pattern of database queries as evidence of ongoing danger. And the system that enabled the surveillance continues to operate on the same terms after the case concludes. Chuck Wexler, executive director of the Police Executive Research Forum, acknowledged the gap in the Washington Post investigation: "Very often a technology will be farther ahead of policy, and that's what has happened, I think, with license plate readers." That gap is not narrowing on its own. Flock's network is larger today than at any point in its history. The warrant requirement that would make each of the 50 documented searches a criminal violation at the moment of query -- rather than a policy violation discovered months later -- does not exist. What Drivers Can Do Right Now The options available to a driver who suspects she has been tracked through an ALPR network are limited but real. Check HaveIBeenFlocked.com by entering your license plate number. The site aggregates publicly available audit logs from departments that release them through public records requests. It cannot show you searches from departments that do not make their logs public -- but it will show you any queries that appear in the records it holds. File a public records request with your local police department asking for all Flock Safety audit logs showing searches of your vehicle's plate number. You are generally entitled to this information under state public records laws, though departments vary in their responsiveness and the completeness of what they produce. Contact your state legislator about ALPR data governance. Six states -- California, Colorado, Washington, Utah, Kentucky, and Maine -- have enacted some form of ALPR-specific legislation; most have not. A mandatory warrant requirement for individual officer searches is the most direct protection against the pattern the Washington Post documented. Know the reporting path. If you believe a law enforcement officer has used ALPR or any police database to stalk you, you can report the conduct to your state attorney general's office, your state's law enforcement certification board (which handles officer misconduct), or the FBI's public corruption division -- all of which operate independent of the department employing the officer. The IJ's Plate Privacy Project (plateprivacy.com) provides resources for victims and communities challenging warrantless ALPR use. Frequently Asked Questions Can a police officer legally track my vehicle through Flock Safety's network without a warrant? In most of the United States, yes. No federal law requires officers to obtain a warrant before querying an ALPR database, and no federal standard mandates that searches be tied to an active investigation or case number. A handful of states -- including California, Colorado, Utah, and Washington -- have enacted laws that impose warrant requirements for certain ALPR uses, particularly real-time tracking. The constitutional status of comprehensive ALPR network queries is currently being litigated in the Fourth Circuit (Schmidt v. City of Norfolk), where the ACLU and EFF argue that the Supreme Court's 2018 Carpenter ruling should require a warrant for historical vehicle location records at scale. The Supreme Court has not decided an ALPR case. How can I find out if my license plate has been searched in Flock Safety's database? Go to HaveIBeenFlocked.com and enter your license plate number. The site aggregates publicly available police audit logs from departments that release them. It cannot show searches from departments that keep their logs private or have not been the subject of public records requests -- so a clean result does not guarantee you have not been searched. For a more complete picture, file a public records request with your local police department asking specifically for all Flock Safety audit log entries showing searches of your plate number. Why can't victims simply report this to police? In most of the 50 documented cases, the officer conducting the surveillance worked for the same department the victim would need to approach. Marci Bakely put it plainly after discovering that Braselton's police chief had queried her plate 600 times: "Who do you turn the police chief in to?" External reporting options include the state attorney general's office, the state law enforcement certification board, and the FBI's public corruption division. The Institute for Justice's Plate Privacy Project (plateprivacy.com) tracks ongoing cases and provides resources for victims and communities challenging warrantless ALPR surveillance. Would a warrant requirement have prevented the cases documented in the Washington Post investigation? Almost certainly in most of them. Each of the 50 documented misuse cases involved an officer searching a plate for personal reasons -- not in connection with a crime under investigation. A warrant requirement ties each search to a judge's determination of probable cause. Without that requirement, the only check on misuse is departmental audit -- which, in most documented cases, caught the pattern only after victims reported the conduct. The Institute for Justice's attorney Michael Soyfer stated: "Without the constitutional safeguard of a warrant requirement, that predictably allows officers to abuse their access to these systems for things like stalking romantic partners. Requiring a warrant would force officers to show probable cause before allowing access to ALPR camera network databases."

pendingReview.title: Man jailed after allegedly recording 5-year-old child, adult women while using the bathroom
pendingReview.description: Charges are allegations only. All arrested persons are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. WEBER COUNTY, Utah (ABC4) -- A man was jailed after allegedly recording a 5-year-old child and other adult women while they were using the bathroom at a wedding. Tyrus Nawaikalae Stephens, 22, has been charged with voyeurism-recording a child under the age of 14 (third-degree felony) and voyeurism-recording (class A misdemeanor).
